question: How are LLMs aligned with user instructions and human preferences, through SFT, RLHF (reward model plus PPO), DPO and related refinements, and inference-time methods?
contributions: A unified derivation of SFT loss masking, reward modelling with Bradley-Terry, A2C/PPO for RLHF, and DPO, in one notation
Refinements: listwise/pointwise/fine-grained rewards, reward ensembles, AI feedback, process supervision, Best-of-N

limits: No experiments of its own: every empirical number is quoted from other work, and the chapter gives no hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size, beta, epsilon, N for Best-of-N) for any method.
Sparse-reward discussion and the advantage-as-shaped-reward link (Eq 4.64-4.66) are argued, not measured.
Authors concede no fully satisfactory solution to reward overoptimisation exists (Sec 4.4.1.4) and weak-to-strong generalisation still needs investigation.
Dated or absent: no GRPO, RLVR/verifiable-reward RL, KTO/IPO/SimPO, constitutional AI or LLM-as-judge detail; o1/o3 are mentioned only in passing; PPO is presented as the main RLHF algorithm.

Notation slips: text says 'the model presented in Eq. (4.47)' where the surrogate is Eq. (4.45); Fig 4.4 caption cites Wang et al., 2023b while the text cites Wang et al., 2023d for self-instruct; the PPO reference policy is called theta_ref in the text and theta_old in Fig 4.9; Eq. 4.45 is written without the baseline-subtracted clip, and Eq. 4.52 is a sequence log-ratio penalty rather than a per-token KL.
Eq. 4.41/4.40 minimise a loss while Eq. 4.28 is written as a gradient to ascend; sign conventions differ between the policy-gradient and loss forms.
The PDF has no reference list, so cited works cannot be matched to arXiv ids from this source.
practices: Compute the SFT loss only on output tokens: run the forward pass on the concatenated [x,y] and zero the loss on x (Sec 4.2.1, Fig 4.2).
For multi-turn chat SFT, represent the whole conversation as one sequence and mask the loss on every user turn, so one pass trains all K responses (Eq 4.6-4.7, Fig 4.3).
Mitigate overfitting and forgetting in SFT with regularisation, early stopping, a smaller learning rate and diverse source data (Sec 4.2.1).
Use parameter-efficient fine-tuning when full SFT is too costly (Sec 4.2.1).
Build SFT data by writing prompt templates for existing NLP tasks and filling slots from labelled datasets, by scraping natural QA data, or by crowdsourcing (Sec 4.2.2.1).
Use self-instruct (task pool, sample instructions, generate new instruction, generate sample, filter) to bootstrap more SFT data from a small seed set (Sec 4.2.2.2).
For classification tasks, generate the input from instruction plus a chosen output (input inversion) to avoid class-skewed synthetic data (Sec 4.2.2.2).
Prefer smaller higher-quality SFT sets, selected by an LLM quality rater, heuristics or influence, over scaling raw volume (Sec 4.2.3).
Train the reward model as a decoder plus a linear head on the last-token state, with the Bradley-Terry pairwise loss, then score each (x,y) independently during RL (Sec 4.3.2).
Initialise the reward and value models from the pre-trained LLM, and the reference and policy models from the instruction-tuned model (Sec 4.3.3).
Subtract a value-function baseline (advantage / TD error) and clip the importance ratio, plus a log-ratio penalty to the reference policy, in PPO (Sec 4.3.3).
Prefer pairwise or listwise reward training over pointwise regression because human scores are noisy; pointwise suits abundant, consistent labels (Sec 4.4.1.1).
Combine several reward models (ensembles, aspect-specific, off-the-shelf LLMs) to reduce overoptimisation (Sec 4.4.1.4).
Use DPO when a reward model and online sampling are too costly; use PPO-style online RL when exploration and generalisation matter (Sec 4.4.2).
Make AI-feedback preference data diverse (different LLMs, prompts, demonstrations) and use label-token probabilities as soft labels; use human feedback for subjective values (Sec 4.4.3).
For reasoning tasks, supervise intermediate steps (process-based) rather than only the final answer, and annotate steps the model is confident about but that are wrong (Sec 4.4.4).
Use Best-of-N reranking or rejection-sampling fine-tuning as cheap alignment, and keep the N-best list diverse (Sec 4.4.5).

terms.definition: the process of aligning model outputs with human expectations
tune the LLM to accurately respond to user instructions and intentions
further training on task-specific instructions paired with expected outputs, with loss computed only over the output tokens conditioned on the input
prompt an LLM to create a new instruction by learning from other instructions, then fill in the other fields and generate outputs
learning primarily occurs during pre-training, and the subsequent fine-tuning or alignment phase does not significantly contribute to the underlying knowledge base of an LLM
a machine learning method is sample efficient if it can learn effectively from a small number of training examples
using smaller, less complex models to improve the training of larger, more complex models
max{0, (P_weak->strong - P_weak)/(P_ceiling - P_weak)}: how much of the gap between ceiling and weak-model performance the weak-to-strong model recovers
LLMs learn from comparisons of model outputs using reward models
the probability distribution over tokens the LLM predicts given the preceding context, pi(a|s)=Pr(y_t|x,y<t)
A(s_t,a_t) = sum_{k>=t} r_k - V(s_t), the relative benefit of action a_t compared to the expected value of following the policy from s_t; also the TD error r_t + gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t)
generalises Bradley-Terry to rankings of many items, with worth alpha(y)=exp(r(x,y))
over-aligning LLMs with an imperfect reward proxy decreases performance; Goodhart's law: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure
direct preference optimization: optimises the policy directly on preference pairs with no explicit reward model, via the implicit reward r=beta log(pi/pi_ref)+beta log Z
outcome-based supervises only when the end result is verified; process-based supervises all intermediate steps in addition to the last
use the reward model to select the best one from N alternative outputs generated by the LLM
select the best outputs from N-best lists with the reward model, then fine-tune the LLM on them

code.snippet: log Pr(x,y) = log Pr(x) [set to 0] + log Pr(y|x) [loss computation]
multi-turn: loss on log Pr(y_k | x_1,y_1,...,x_k) only; user-turn terms set to 0
r(x,y)=h_last W_r;  Pr(ya>yb|x)=Sigmoid(r(x,ya)-r(x,yb));  L_r = -E log Pr(ya>yb|x)
Clip = min(ratio*A, bound(ratio,1-eps,1+eps)*A);  U_ppo-clip = U_clip - beta*Penalty;  Penalty = sum_t log pi_theta(a_t|s_t) - sum_t log pi_ref(a_t|s_t)
L_list = -E[ 2/(N(N-1)) sum_{ya>yb} log Pr(ya>yb|x) ];  Plackett-Luce: log Pr(Y|x)=sum_k log Pr(y_jk | x, Y>=k)
f = gamma Phi(s_{t+1}) - Phi(s_t); with Phi=V: r' = r + gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t)
r(x,y)=beta(log pi_theta/pi_ref + log Z(x));  L_dpo = -E log Sigmoid(beta log pi_theta(ya|x)/pi_ref(ya|x) - beta log pi_theta(yb|x)/pi_ref(yb|x))
process reward r(x,y)=sum_k log Pr(correct|x,y<=k);  BoN: y_best = argmax_{y in N-best} r(x,y)
